source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: ‘Slave’ retains Paul’s ownership language; it is not softened to hired service.
‘From faith to faith’ is compact and disputed. The main text preserves the phrase rather than choosing one exhaustive explanation.

Paul’s female/male and natural/contrary language is translated directly. The passage is situated within the argument that turns in 2:1 toward the judging reader; the note does not add a modern political or doctrinal verdict.
vocabulary: Slave, a person owned by another; also used metaphorically for complete allegiance.

notes: The direct address turns the charge back on anyone who condemns others while practicing the same things.
Gentiles without Torah are described as sometimes doing its requirements, with conscience and competing thoughts bearing witness.
The argument contrasts merely outward circumcision with inward, Spirit-worked faithfulness; it does not erase Jewish identity or the Law’s prior value.
vocabulary: Repentance, a changed mind and direction.

notes: The same word-family can describe human unfaithfulness and God’s faithfulness; the repetition is retained.
The Greek phrase can mean ‘faithfulness of Jesus Christ’ or ‘faith in Jesus Christ.’ The main text chooses the former while the following phrase explicitly names all who believe.
The term translated ‘atoning sacrifice’ can also evoke the mercy seat, the place of atonement. The main text does not exhaust the image.
The prepositions differ, but Paul identifies one God and one faith rather than two ways of justification.
vocabulary: Declare righteous, vindicate, or set right.
Redemption or release secured at a cost.

notes: ‘According to the flesh’ can modify Abraham as physical ancestor; the sentence is rendered with that natural connection.
Circumcision is a sign and seal received after Abraham’s faith, allowing Paul to describe him as father of believing people in both groups.
The verse names Abraham’s aged body and Sarah’s womb without blaming either person for infertility.
Both clauses use ‘because of’; the compact parallel does not require that Jesus’ resurrection was caused by an already completed human justification.
vocabulary: Seal, a mark of confirmation or ownership.
Heir, one who receives an inheritance.

notes: The pinned Greek reads ‘we have peace,’ an indicative statement. Some ancient witnesses support ‘let us have peace.’
The final phrase is rendered ‘because all sinned.’ It has also been interpreted ‘in whom all sinned’; that alternative materially affects inherited-sin readings.
Adam is called a pattern of the coming one; the following verses develop both correspondence and greater contrast.
Paul’s parallel uses ‘all’ and ‘the many’ within the Adam/Christ comparison. The translation leaves the scope visible without supplying a doctrinal system.
Baptism is described as participation in Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection-shaped new life.
The old self and body ruled by sin are crucified so that slavery to sin ends; ‘freed’ in verse 7 represents a legal justification verb in this context.
Paul deliberately uses ancient slavery as a severe metaphor for mastery and obedience. The translation retains the image while not treating the brutal institution as morally harmless.
The contrast is between wages earned from sin and God’s unearned gracious gift.
vocabulary: Newness or a new quality of life.
